# facett_map - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-map/^0.1/

## Expand description

**facett-map** — a geo viewer: a **point** layer plus a **vector basemap**
(roads / coastlines / water as lines, or closed rings drawn as filled
silhouettes + crisp outlines). Plots `(lon, lat)` with **Web Mercator** (the
projection osm-viewer’s `gpu_backend::CpuBackend` uses), so it lines up with
real tiles.

Two render paths share one `ui()`:

- **CPU painter**(default) — points as dots; ways as themed line segments, or, when a way carries a- `fill`, as a filled silhouette with a crisp outline on top. Always available, headless-testable, never panics.
- **wgpu GPU kernel**(feature- `wgpu`) — the upload-once compute-cull +- `draw_indirect`pipeline- **ported from katana-osm’s**(- `osm-viewer`- `render::gpu::GpuMapRenderer`/- `MapPaintCallback`). All way geometry is uploaded once; pan/zoom only updates a uniform; the GPU frustum-culls every frame. (The GPU path draws the line basemap; filled silhouettes still draw on the CPU on top — the rabbit/synthetic case never needs the GPU cull.)

Source-agnostic: the host loads points + ways (e.g. korp’s map load from
osm-katana GeoParquet, via [`facett_osm::read_points`] / `read_ways`) and
hands them here. **Graceful:** no ways → just points (the original behavior —
the point-only [ MapView::new](https://docs.rs/struct.MapView.html#method.new) API is unchanged). When the host has no real
basemap it can hand a

*synthetic*one; facett-demo feeds the

**znippy rabbit**silhouette (see

`facett_core::rabbit`) as the synthetic test basemap.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use style::`- [Lod](https://docs.rs/style/enum.Lod.html);
- `pub use style::`- [MapPalette](https://docs.rs/style/struct.MapPalette.html);
- `pub use style::`- [WayStyle](https://docs.rs/style/struct.WayStyle.html);
- `pub use style::`- [classify](https://docs.rs/style/fn.classify.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [index](https://docs.rs/index/index.html)
- Spatial / LOD index over `Way``osm-viewer/src/render/index.rs`. The source uses`static_aabb2d_index`for a packed Hilbert R-tree; facett keeps the**LOD-tier split**(the part the GPU path actually needs —`gpu_ways()`walks all tiers to build the upload- once vertex buffer) and provides a dependency-free brute-force`query_visible`for the CPU fallback. On-screen the GPU compute shader does the real per-frame frustum cull, so a heavyweight CPU R-tree is not required.
- [project](https://docs.rs/project/index.html)
- Web-Mercator projection helpers, ported from katana-osm’s
`osm-viewer/src/render/project.rs`. Mercator unit space is`[0,1]²`(x: lon −180→+180, y: north→south), the space the GPU shader expects.
- [style](https://docs.rs/style/index.html)
- Per-OSM-tag styling for the vector basemap, ported from katana-osm’s
`osm-viewer/src/render/style.rs`and re-keyed onto the facett`Theme`
- [tessellate](https://docs.rs/tessellate/index.html)
- **Polygon fill tessellation**for the vector basemap. OSM area rings (lakes, parks, coastline-bounded land, building footprints) are almost never convex, so- `egui::Shape::convex_polygon`mis-fills them (it fans from the first vertex → spurious triangles spill outside a concave ring). This module triangulates an arbitrary simple polygon with- **ear clipping**— O(n²), dependency-free, no rayon — and emits an- `egui::Mesh`the painter draws as a correct flat fill. For the small per-way rings a basemap carries this is plenty fast, and it is exact for concave shapes (where- `convex_polygon`is not).

- [Way](https://docs.rs/struct.Way.html)

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_BUILDING_LEVELS.html)- BUILDING_ - LEVELS
- Default storeys assumed for a building with **no**height tag — a low ~2-storey town building (so the bulk of an untagged OSM town reads as a low skyline, not uniform towers). The 3D extruder uses this when`Way::height_m``None`.
- [METRES_](https://docs.rs/constant.METRES_PER_LEVEL.html)- PER_ - LEVEL
- Metres per building storey when deriving a height from `building:levels`(a typical floor-to-floor of ~3 m). Shared by the tag parser + the 3D extruder.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [mercator](https://docs.rs/fn.mercator.html)
- Web Mercator, normalised to `0..1`(x east, y south). Matches osm-viewer.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_building_height_m.html)- building_ - height_ - m
- Parse an OSM building height (in metres) from its tags: `height=<m>`(an explicit metre value, possibly suffixed`m`) takes priority; otherwise`building:levels`×`METRES_PER_LEVEL``None`when neither tag is present or parses (the extruder then falls back to a default). Tolerant of the common`"30 m"`/`"12.5"`/`"3"`spellings.

# parquet - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/parquet/^58/

## Expand description

This crate contains the official Native Rust implementation of
[Apache Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/), part of
the [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/) project.
The crate provides a number of APIs to read and write Parquet files,
covering a range of use cases.

Please see the [parquet crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/parquet)
page for feature flags and tips to improve performance.

[§](https://docs.rs#format-overview)Format Overview

Parquet is a columnar format, which means that unlike row formats like [CSV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comma-separated_values), values are
iterated along columns instead of rows. Parquet is similar in spirit to [Arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/index.html), but
focuses on storage efficiency whereas Arrow prioritizes compute efficiency.

Parquet files are partitioned for scalability. Each file contains metadata, along with zero or more “row groups”, each row group containing one or more columns. The APIs in this crate reflect this structure.

Data in Parquet files is strongly typed and differentiates between logical
and physical types (see [ schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)). In addition, Parquet files may contain
other metadata, such as statistics, which can be used to optimize reading
(see

[). For more details about the Parquet format itself, see the](https://docs.rs/file/metadata/index.html)

`file::metadata`[Parquet spec](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/README.md#file-format)

[§](https://docs.rs#apis)APIs

This crate exposes a number of APIs for different use-cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#metadata-and-schema)Metadata and Schema

The [ schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html) module provides APIs to work with Parquet schemas. The

[module provides APIs to work with Parquet metadata.](https://docs.rs/file/metadata/index.html)

`file::metadata`[§](https://docs.rs#reading-and-writing-arrow-arrow-feature)Reading and Writing Arrow (`arrow` feature)

The [ arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/index.html) module supports reading and writing Parquet data to/from
Arrow

[es. Using Arrow is simple and performant, and allows workloads to leverage the wide range of data transforms provided by the](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`[arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/index.html)crate, and by the ecosystem of

[Arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/index.html)compatible systems.

Most users will use [ ArrowWriter](https://docs.rs/arrow/arrow_writer/struct.ArrowWriter.html) for writing and

[for reading from synchronous IO sources such as files or in-memory buffers.](https://docs.rs/arrow/arrow_reader/type.ParquetRecordBatchReaderBuilder.html)

`ParquetRecordBatchReaderBuilder`Lower level APIs include

- `ParquetPushDecoder`
- `ArrowColumnWriter`
- `RowFilter`

[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-content-defined-chunking)EXPERIMENTAL: Content-Defined Chunking

[ ArrowWriter](https://docs.rs/arrow/arrow_writer/struct.ArrowWriter.html) supports content-defined chunking (CDC), which creates data page
boundaries based on content rather than fixed sizes. CDC enables efficient
deduplication in content-addressable storage (CAS) systems: when the same data
appears in successive file versions, it will produce identical byte sequences that
CAS backends can deduplicate.

Enable CDC via [ WriterProperties](https://docs.rs/file/properties/struct.WriterProperties.html):

```
let props = WriterProperties::builder()
    .set_content_defined_chunking(Some(CdcOptions::default()))
    .build();
```
See [ CdcOptions](https://docs.rs/file/properties/struct.CdcOptions.html) for chunk size and normalization parameters.

[§](https://docs.rs#async-reading-and-writing-arrow-arrow-feature--async-feature)`async` Reading and Writing Arrow (`arrow` feature + `async` feature)

The [ async_reader](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_reader/index.html) and

[modules provide async APIs to read and write](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_writer/index.html)

`async_writer`[es asynchronously.](https://docs.rs/arrow/latest/arrow/array/struct.RecordBatch.html)

`RecordBatch`Most users will use [ AsyncArrowWriter](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_writer/struct.AsyncArrowWriter.html) for writing and

[for reading. When the](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_reader/type.ParquetRecordBatchStreamBuilder.html)

`ParquetRecordBatchStreamBuilder``object_store` feature is enabled, [provides efficient integration with object storage services such as S3 via the](https://docs.rs/arrow/async_reader/struct.ParquetObjectReader.html)

`ParquetObjectReader`[object_store](https://docs.rs/object_store/latest/object_store/)crate, automatically optimizing IO based on any predicates or projections provided.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant-logical-type-variant_experimental-feature)Variant Logical Type (`variant_experimental` feature)

The [ variant](https://docs.rs/variant/index.html) module supports reading and writing Parquet files
with the

[Variant Binary Encoding](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/VariantEncoding.md)logical type, which can represent semi-structured data such as JSON efficiently.

[§](https://docs.rs#readwrite-parquet-directly)Read/Write Parquet Directly

Workloads needing finer-grained control, or to avoid a dependence on arrow,
can use the APIs in [ file](https://docs.rs/file/index.html) directly. These APIs  are harder to use
as they directly use the underlying Parquet data model, and require knowledge
of the Parquet format, including the details of

[Dremel](https://research.google/pubs/pub36632/)record shredding and

[Logical Types](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/LogicalTypes.md).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [arrow](https://docs.rs/arrow/index.html)- `arrow`
- API for reading/writing Arrow `RecordBatch``Array`
- [basic](https://docs.rs/basic/index.html)
- Contains Rust mappings for Thrift definition. This module contains only mappings for thrift
enums and unions. Thrift structs are handled elsewhere.
Refer to `parquet.thrift`
- [bloom_](https://docs.rs/bloom_filter/index.html)- filter
- Bloom filter implementation specific to Parquet, as described
in the [spec](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/BloomFilter.md).
- [column](https://docs.rs/column/index.html)
- Low level column reader and writer APIs.
- [data_](https://docs.rs/data_type/index.html)- type
- Data types that connect Parquet physical types with their Rust-specific representations.
- [errors](https://docs.rs/errors/index.html)
- Common Parquet errors and macros.
- [file](https://docs.rs/file/index.html)
- APIs for reading parquet data.
- [format](https://docs.rs/format/index.html)- Deprecated
- Automatically generated code from the Parquet thrift definition.
- [record](https://docs.rs/record/index.html)
- Contains record-based API for reading Parquet files.
- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- Parquet schema definitions and methods to print and parse schema.
- [thrift](https://docs.rs/thrift/index.html)
- Custom thrift definitions
- [utf8](https://docs.rs/utf8/index.html)
- `check_valid_utf8`
- [variant](https://docs.rs/variant/index.html)- `variant_experimental`
- ⚠️ Experimental Support for reading and writing `Variant`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

# facett_osm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-osm/0.1.10/facett_osm/index.html

## Expand description

**facett-osm** — read **OSM GeoParquet** (the `osm2geoparquet` / katana-osm
output) into facett geometry. Each row’s `geometry` column is **WKB** — a
`Point` for nodes, a `LineString`/`Polygon` for ways — which we decode to
`(lon, lat)` points and hand to [ facett_map::MapView](https://docs.rs/facett-map/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_map/struct.MapView.html). This is how facett
gets real OSM data (millions of points) for the map component + its tests.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_wkb.html)- wkb
- Decode a WKB geometry blob, appending every `(lon, lat)`vertex to`out`. Handles Point (1), LineString (2), Polygon (3); ignores Z/M + SRID flags.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_wkb_coords.html)- wkb_ - coords
- Decode a single WKB blob into **one geometry’s**`(lon, lat)`vertices (Point → 1 vertex, LineString → its line, Polygon → its exterior ring), preserving the geometry as a unit (unlike`decode_wkb``read_ways``katana_osm_shared::geometry::decode_coords`.
- [map_](https://docs.rs/fn.map_view.html)- view
- Read a GeoParquet straight into a `facett_map::MapView`
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_points.html)- points
- Read up to `max``(lon, lat)`points from a GeoParquet file’s`geometry`(WKB) column. Works on`osm2geoparquet`’s`nodes.parquet`(Points) and`ways.parquet`(LineStrings → their vertices).
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_points_bytes.html)- points_ - bytes
- Like `read_points`**in-memory**GeoParquet (the bytes of a`nodes.parquet`). This is the filesystem-free path the wasm web demo uses: it`include_bytes!`s a clipped region into the binary and decodes it here (the browser has no`std::fs`). Any`Into<Bytes>`works (`&'static [u8]`,`Vec<u8>`).
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_ways.html)- ways
- Read **ways**(LineString / Polygon geometries) from an`osm2geoparquet``ways.parquet`— the SAME WKB`geometry`column`read_points``tags`column for styling. Each row → a`facett_map::Way``(lon, lat)`, projected to Mercator, classified by its OSM tags through`theme`.`max`caps the number of ways (0 = unlimited). Rows with <2 vertices are skipped (graceful — no panic on a degenerate geometry).
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_ways_bytes.html)- ways_ - bytes
- Like `read_ways`**in-memory**`ways.parquet`(the bytes the wasm web demo`include_bytes!`s — no filesystem in the browser).

[175](#175)    let reader = ParquetRecordBatchReaderBuilder::try_new(src)
[176](#176)        .map_err(|e| format!("parquet: {e}"))?
[177](#177)        .with_batch_size(16384)
[178](#178)        .build()
[179](#179)        .map_err(|e| format!("parquet: {e}"))?;
[180](#180)
[181](#181)    let cap = if max == 0 { usize::MAX } else { max };
[182](#182)    let mut out: Vec<Way> = Vec::new();
[183](#183)    for batch in reader {
[184](#184)        let batch = batch.map_err(|e| format!("read: {e}"))?;
[185](#185)        let geom = batch
[186](#186)            .column_by_name("geometry")
[187](#187)            .and_then(|c| c.as_any().downcast_ref::<BinaryArray>())
[188](#188)            .ok_or("no Binary `geometry` (WKB) column")?;
[189](#189)        let tags_col = batch
[190](#190)            .column_by_name("tags")
[191](#191)            .and_then(|c| c.as_any().downcast_ref::<StringArray>());
[192](#192)        for i in 0..geom.len() {
[193](#193)            if geom.is_null(i) {
[194](#194)                continue;
[195](#195)            }
[196](#196)            let coords = decode_wkb_coords(geom.value(i));
[197](#197)            if coords.len() < 2 {
[198](#198)                continue; }
[200](#200)            let tags = tags_col
[201](#201)                .filter(|t| !t.is_null(i))
[202](#202)                .map(|t| parse_tags(t.value(i)))
[203](#203)                .unwrap_or_default();
[204](#204)            if let Some(w) = Way::from_lonlat(0, &coords, &tags, theme) {
[205](#205)                out.push(w);
[206](#206)                if out.len() >= cap {
[207](#207)                    return Ok(out);
[208](#208)                }
[209](#209)            }
[210](#210)        }
[211](#211)    }

# decode_wkb_coords in facett_osm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-osm/0.1.10/facett_osm/fn.decode_wkb_coords.html

## Expand description

Decode a single WKB blob into **one geometry’s** `(lon, lat)` vertices
(Point → 1 vertex, LineString → its line, Polygon → its exterior ring),
preserving the geometry as a unit (unlike [ decode_wkb](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_wkb.html), which flattens many
geometries into one buffer). This is what

[needs to build a per-way polyline. Mirrors](https://docs.rs/fn.read_ways.html)

`read_ways``katana_osm_shared::geometry::decode_coords`.

---

# read_points_bytes in facett_osm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-osm/0.1.10/facett_osm/fn.read_points_bytes.html

## Expand description

Like [ read_points](https://docs.rs/fn.read_points.html) but reads an

**in-memory**GeoParquet (the bytes of a

`nodes.parquet`). This is the filesystem-free path the wasm web demo uses: it
`include_bytes!`s a clipped region into the binary and decodes it here (the
browser has no `std::fs`). Any `Into<Bytes>` works (`&'static [u8]`, `Vec<u8>`).

# Way in facett_map - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-map/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_map/struct.Way.html

    pub osm_id: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html),

}## Expand description

One vector-basemap way. Carries **both** representations so the two render
paths coexist:

- `points`/- `bbox`— vertices in- **Mercator unit**space (- `[0,1]²`,- `f32`) + the precomputed Mercator bbox. This is what the GPU geometry builder + the GPU/CPU frustum cull consume (the ported osm-viewer line basemap).
- `lonlat`— the source- `(lon, lat)`WGS-84 vertices, kept so the CPU painter can fit + draw- **filled silhouettes**(the synthetic-rabbit closed-ring look) without re-deriving them.

`style` is the themed classification (colour/width/LOD/kind) used by the GPU
path; `fill`, `stroke`, `width`, `kind` drive the CPU silhouette/outline.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/facett_map/lib.rs.html#186-212)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/facett_map/lib.rs.html#186-212)

Build a way from `(lon, lat)` WGS-84 vertices, projecting to Mercator unit
space and computing the bbox. `tags` classify it through `theme`. This is
the **real-OSM** constructor: an **area** way (water / park / landuse /
building) whose geometry is a closed ring becomes a **filled polygon**
(themed fill + a crisp outline); a **line** way (road / path / coastline),
or an unclosed area, strokes only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/facett_map/lib.rs.html#217-221)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/facett_map/lib.rs.html#217-221)

A stroked-only polyline way with an explicit colour/width (the synthetic
basemap path; no tag classification). Carried at `Lod::Country` so it
always shows when the index/GPU cull is involved.

# m4_rs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/m4-rs/^0.1/

## Expand description

`m4-rs` — forensic-parity GNU m4 reimplementation. The workspace crate: it ships the `m4-rs`
CLI binary and re-exports the member crates so `cargo install m4-rs` gives the tool and
`cargo add m4-rs` gives the engine.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [m4_casefile_rs](https://docs.rs/m4-casefile-rs/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/m4_casefile_rs/index.html);

- `pub use`- [m4_rs_cli](https://docs.rs/m4-rs-cli/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/m4_rs_cli/index.html);
- `pub use`- [m4_rs_core](https://docs.rs/m4-rs-core/0.1.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/m4_rs_core/index.html);

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

# sha2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sha2/^0.10/

## Expand description

An implementation of the [SHA-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2) cryptographic hash algorithms.

There are 6 standard algorithms specified in the SHA-2 standard: [ Sha224](https://docs.rs/type.Sha224.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/type.Sha256.html)

`Sha256`[,](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512_224.html)

`Sha512_224`[,](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512_256.html)

`Sha512_256`[, and](https://docs.rs/type.Sha384.html)

`Sha384`[.](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512.html)

`Sha512`Algorithmically, there are only 2 core algorithms: SHA-256 and SHA-512. All other algorithms are just applications of these with different initial hash values, and truncated to different digest bit lengths. The first two algorithms in the list are based on SHA-256, while the last four are based on SHA-512.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#one-shot-api)One-shot API

```
use hex_literal::hex;
use sha2::{Sha256, Digest};
let result = Sha256::digest(b"hello world");
assert_eq!(result[..], hex!("
    b94d27b9934d3e08a52e52d7da7dabfac484efe37a5380ee9088f7ace2efcde9
")[..]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#incremental-api)Incremental API

```
use hex_literal::hex;
use sha2::{Sha256, Sha512, Digest};
// create a Sha256 object
let mut hasher = Sha256::new();
// write input message
hasher.update(b"hello world");
// read hash digest and consume hasher
let result = hasher.finalize();
assert_eq!(result[..], hex!("
    b94d27b9934d3e08a52e52d7da7dabfac484efe37a5380ee9088f7ace2efcde9
")[..]);
// same for Sha512
let mut hasher = Sha512::new();
hasher.update(b"hello world");
let result = hasher.finalize();
assert_eq!(result[..], hex!("
    309ecc489c12d6eb4cc40f50c902f2b4d0ed77ee511a7c7a9bcd3ca86d4cd86f
    989dd35bc5ff499670da34255b45b0cfd830e81f605dcf7dc5542e93ae9cd76f
")[..]);
```
Also see [RustCrypto/hashes](https://github.com/RustCrypto/hashes) readme.

- [Sha512](https://docs.rs/struct.Sha512VarCore.html)- VarCore
- Core block-level SHA-512 hasher with variable output size.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- Raw SHA-256 compression function.
- [compress512](https://docs.rs/fn.compress512.html)- `compress`
- Raw SHA-512 compression function.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

–mode=install / –mode=clean            -> best-effort copy / rm macro_overrides  m4 macro definitions injected AFTER aclocal.m4 (so they override the project’s third-party
definitions) and BEFORE configure.ac. autoconf-rs cannot yet correctly expand some standard
third-party macros (notably pkg.m4’s PKG_CHECK_MODULES, whose internals leak
`pkg_default`/`glib_minimum` -> shell syntax errors). We replace them with clean, self-contained
shell that does the real work: run pkg-config at configure time, set PFX_CFLAGS/PFX_LIBS, and
record `@PFX_CFLAGS@`/`@PFX_LIBS@` substitutions into conf_subst.sed (consumed when config files
are created, mirroring confdefs.h -> config.h).

[233](#233)pub fn libtool_script() -> &'static str {
[240](#240)    r##"#! /bin/sh
[241](#241)# Minimal libtool wrapper generated by autoconf-rs (GNU-free).
[242](#242)mode=
[243](#243)for a in "$@"; do case $a in --mode=*) mode=${a#--mode=} ;; esac; done
[244](#244)# Drop libtool's own options from the positional params, preserving every other arg EXACTLY.
[245](#245)# The old `cmd="$cmd $a"` + `eval set -- $cmd` re-split and re-evaluated the args, stripping the
[246](#246)# literal quotes from `-DFOO=\"/path\"` defines -> gcc saw `-DFOO=/path` -> `<command-line>: expected
[247](#247)# expression before '/' token` (a systemic make-stage failure for libtool projects with path defines,
[248](#248)# e.g. pup-volume-monitor's -DPUP_VM_SCRIPTS_DIR). Rotate kept args to the end so quoting survives.
[249](#249)_lt_n=$#
[250](#250)while test $_lt_n -gt 0; do
[251](#251)  _lt_a=$1; shift; _lt_n=$((_lt_n-1))
[252](#252)  case $_lt_a in
[253](#253)    --mode=*|--tag=*|--silent|--quiet|--verbose|--no-silent|--preserve-dup-deps) continue ;;
[254](#254)  esac
[255](#255)  set -- "$@" "$_lt_a"
[256](#256)done
[257](#257)
[258](#258)case $mode in
[259](#259)compile)
[260](#260)  comp=$1; shift
[261](#261)  flags=; src=; lo=
[262](#262)  while test $# -gt 0; do
[263](#263)    case $1 in
[264](#264)      -o) shift; lo=$1 ;;
[265](#265)      -c) ;;
[266](#266)      *) flags="$flags $1"; case $1 in *.c|*.cc|*.cpp|*.cxx|*.C|*.s|*.S) src=$1 ;; esac ;;
[267](#267)    esac
[268](#268)    shift
[269](#269)  done
[270](#270)  test -n "$lo" || lo=`echo "$src" | sed 's/\.[^.]*$/.lo/'`
[271](#271)  obj=`echo "$lo" | sed 's/\.lo$/.o/'`
[272](#272)  dir=`dirname "$lo"`; base=`basename "$obj"`
[273](#273)  mkdir -p "$dir/.libs"
[274](#274)  $comp $flags -fPIC -DPIC -c -o "$dir/.libs/$base" || exit 1
[275](#275)  $comp $flags -c -o "$obj" 2>/dev/null || cp "$dir/.libs/$base" "$obj"
[276](#276)  { echo "# $lo - libtool object (autoconf-rs)"
[277](#277)    echo "pic_object='.libs/$base'"
[278](#278)    echo "non_pic_object='$base'"; } > "$lo"
[279](#279)  exit 0
[280](#280)  ;;
[281](#281)link)
[282](#282)  comp=$1; shift
[283](#283)  out=; inobjs=; deplibs=; rest=; rpaths=
[284](#284)  while test $# -gt 0; do
[285](#285)    case $1 in
[286](#286)      -o) shift; out=$1 ;;
[287](#287)      -rpath|-version-info|-release|-version-number) shift ;;
[288](#288)      -export-dynamic|-module|-avoid-version|-no-undefined|-shared|-static|-no-install|-export-symbols-regex) ;;
[289](#289)      -export-symbols-regex) shift ;;
[290](#290)      *.lo) o=`echo "$1" | sed 's/\.lo$/.o/'`; d=`dirname "$1"`; b=`basename "$o"`; inobjs="$inobjs $d/.libs/$b" ;;
[291](#291)      *.o) inobjs="$inobjs $1" ;;
[292](#292)      # A `-L<dir>/.libs` search path points at an uninstalled libtool library's build dir (e.g. a
[293](#293)      # project links its own lib via `-L./.libs -lfoo` in *_LDFLAGS rather than the .la). Keep the
[294](#294)      # -L and ALSO rpath its absolute path so the program finds libfoo.so at run time (make check).
[295](#295)      -L*.libs|-L*.libs/) rest="$rest $1"; _ldir=${1#-L}; _lab=`cd "$_ldir" 2>/dev/null && pwd`; test -n "$_lab" && rpaths="$rpaths -Wl,-rpath,$_lab" ;;
[296](#296)      # A .la dependency: link `-L<dir>/.libs -l<name>`, AND bake an absolute -rpath to that build
[297](#297)      # `.libs` so the resulting program/library finds the uninstalled .so at RUN time (GNU libtool
[298](#298)      # uses a wrapper script for this; we rpath the build dir instead). Without it, running from the
[299](#299)      # build tree — e.g. `make check` — died: "libfoo.so: cannot open shared object file".
[300](#300)      *.la) la=$1; d=`dirname "$la"`; n=`basename "$la" .la`; deplibs="$deplibs -L$d/.libs -l${n#lib}"; _labs=`cd "$d" 2>/dev/null && pwd`; test -n "$_labs" && rpaths="$rpaths -Wl,-rpath,$_labs/.libs" ;;
[301](#301)      *) rest="$rest $1" ;;
[302](#302)    esac
[303](#303)    shift
[304](#304)  done
[305](#305)  case $out in
[306](#306)  *.la)
[307](#307)    d=`dirname "$out"`; n=`basename "$out" .la`; mkdir -p "$d/.libs"
[308](#308)    ${AR:-ar} cru "$d/.libs/$n.a" $inobjs && ${RANLIB:-ranlib} "$d/.libs/$n.a" 2>/dev/null
[309](#309)    $comp -shared -fPIC -o "$d/.libs/$n.so" $inobjs $deplibs $rpaths $rest 2>/dev/null || :
[310](#310)    { echo "# $out - libtool library (autoconf-rs)"
[311](#311)      echo "dlname='$n.so'"
[312](#312)      echo "library_names='$n.so'"
[313](#313)      echo "old_library='$n.a'"
[314](#314)      echo "installed=no"
[315](#315)      echo "libdir='/usr/local/lib'"; } > "$out"
[316](#316)    ;;
[317](#317)  *)
[318](#318)    mkdir -p .libs
[319](#319)    $comp -o "$out" $inobjs $deplibs $rpaths $rest || exit 1
[320](#320)    ;;
[321](#321)  esac
[322](#322)  exit 0
[323](#323)  ;;
[324](#324)install)
[325](#325)  shift 2>/dev/null
[326](#326)  cp $@ 2>/dev/null || :
[327](#327)  exit 0
[328](#328)  ;;
[329](#329)clean|uninstall)
[330](#330)  exit 0
[331](#331)  ;;
[332](#332)*)
[333](#333)  eval "$cmd"
[334](#334)  ;;
[335](#335)esac
[336](#336)"##

}
```

# autoconf_rs_core::autom4te - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autoconf-rs-core/0.1.52/autoconf_rs_core/autom4te/index.html

## Expand description

autom4te — Caching M4 wrapper for Autoconf.

autom4te is the caching M4 wrapper that autoconf, autoheader, automake, and autoscan all use internally. It caches M4 expansions to avoid re-expansion on subsequent runs.

Cache format divergence: autoconf-rs uses JSON-based cache entries with SHA256 freshness checking, rather than GNU m4 frozen files. This is an admitted divergence (NC.CACHE.FORMAT.1) — semantic caching equivalence, not byte-identical frozen file format.

Receipt family: AC.CLI.AUTOM4TE.* Court: AC.AUTOM4TE.CACHE.1 — caching with –freeze/–reload Status: Phase 5 — caching operational.

# autoconf_rs_core::m4_engine - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autoconf-rs-core/0.1.52/autoconf_rs_core/m4_engine/index.html

## Expand description

M4 macro expansion engine for Autoconf — wraps m4-rs-core.

Uses the forensic-parity m4-rs-core crate for all M4 processing. Autoconf-specific macros (AC_INIT, AC_OUTPUT, etc.) are pre-registered as user macros that expand to the generated shell script text.

M4 expansion output is routed through a DiversionManager for controlled output ordering (lower diversion numbers appear first — critical for AC_REQUIRE dependency ordering).

Receipt family: AC.M4.* Court: AC.M4.DIVERT.WIRED.1 — DiversionManager integrated into pipeline. Current status: Phase 4 — diversion-backed M4 expansion. Panel #1 mandate done.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- M4 expansion engine — wraps m4-rs-core for Autoconf use.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [as_](https://docs.rs/fn.as_case_native.html)- case_ - native
- Native handler for Autoconf’s `AS_CASE(WORD, [PAT1],[ACT1], …, [DEFAULT])`->`case WORD in … esac`. Registered natively because a pure-m4 form can’t work here (recursive m4_shift blows the arg-collection call-depth guard on large cases; unrolling needs $10+, which m4 lacks). Args arrive expanded (arg 0 = WORD; pairs follow; a lone trailing arg is the default).

# autoconf_rs_core::shell_gen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autoconf-rs-core/0.1.52/autoconf_rs_core/shell_gen/index.html

## Expand description

Shell script generator for Autoconf.

Assembles expanded M4 output into a complete POSIX-compliant configure shell script. Handles quoting, escaping, here-documents, variable substitution, and the configure/config.status two-phase output.

Receipt family: AC.SHELL.* Status: Phase 5 — full configure generation with shell sanitization (panel mandate).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Shell](https://docs.rs/struct.ShellGenerator.html)- Generator
- Generates a configure shell script from parsed Autoconf input.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [STD_](https://docs.rs/constant.STD_VAR_DEFAULTS.html)- VAR_ - DEFAULTS
- Standard build-variable defaults emitted inside config.status’s `substitute()`so that the Automake-generated Makefile.in’s`@VAR@`references resolve. Without these, config.status left`@CC@`/`@AR@`/`@top_srcdir@`/`@SET_MAKE@`/… literal ->`make`aborted (“missing separator”). Functional values (cc/ar/…) suffice for`make`; install-time vars use the conventional forms.
- [STD_](https://docs.rs/constant.STD_VAR_SED.html)- VAR_ - SED
- The sed expressions for the standard build variables (double-quoted so the values set by
STD_VAR_DEFAULTS expand when config.status runs). Appended to config.status’s `substitute()`sed.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_config_status_section.html)- config_ - status_ - section
- Generate only the config.status section (substitutions + heredoc). Used when the full oracle-captured template provides the prologue.
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_dynamic_configure.html)- dynamic_ - configure
- Generate a minimal but working configure script with dynamic substitutions. Used when configure.ac has AC_SUBST/AC_CONFIG_FILES/AC_DEFINE/etc. Court: AC.SHELL.DYNAMIC.1
- [sed_](https://docs.rs/fn.sed_subst_expr.html)- subst_ - expr
- Build a SAFE `-e 's|@VAR@|VALUE|g'`sed expr for embedding in a single-quoted shell word. VALUE is sed replacement text. Without care, an AC_SUBST value like`' -I$(srcdir)'`or`'$(MKDIR_P)'`(the surrounding single quotes are part of the captured value) produced`-e 's|@x@|'$(MKDIR_P)'|g'`, where`$(MKDIR_P)`fell OUTSIDE the shell quotes -> command-substituted (`MKDIR_P: command not found`) and the whole sed died -> EMPTY Makefile. We: (1) strip a matched pair of surrounding shell single quotes (automake adds them for shell-assignment; the intended sed value is the inside, e.g.`-I$(srcdir)`, a literal make expands); (2) sed-escape`\ & |`; (3) shell-escape`'`via the`'\''`idiom so the single-quoted word always holds.

# autoconf_rs_core::signal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autoconf-rs-core/0.1.52/autoconf_rs_core/signal/index.html

## Expand description

Signal handling for autoconf-rs — CROSS.040 resolution.

Registers SIGPIPE and SIGINT handlers to enable graceful shutdown instead of default Rust panic-on-signal behavior. Uses raw libc for signal registration (minimal unsafe surface).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [clear_](https://docs.rs/fn.clear_signals.html)- signals
- Reset all signal flags.
- [register_](https://docs.rs/fn.register_signal_handlers.html)- signal_ - handlers
- Register POSIX signal handlers. Called once at startup. Safe because handlers only set atomic flags.
- [sigint_](https://docs.rs/fn.sigint_received.html)- received
- Check if SIGINT was received.
- [sigpipe_](https://docs.rs/fn.sigpipe_received.html)- received
- Check if SIGPIPE was received since last clear.

# autoconf_rs_core::trace_cache - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autoconf-rs-core/0.1.52/autoconf_rs_core/trace_cache/index.html

## Expand description

TraceLog event caching for autom4te/autoheader — panel mandate.

GNU Autoconf’s autom4te caches frozen M4 state (.m4f) so that autoheader can extract AC_DEFINE trace events without re-running the full M4 expansion. This module provides equivalent functionality using JSON-serialized TraceLog events with SHA256 integrity.

Court: AC.TRACE.CACHE.1 Receipt: AC.M4.AUTOM4TE.CACHE.1 (extension)

# libtool_script in autoconf_rs_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autoconf-rs-core/0.1.52/autoconf_rs_core/fn.libtool_script.html

`pub fn libtool_script() -> &'static `[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)## Expand description

A minimal but functional `libtool` wrapper script (autoconf-rs native, GNU-free). Emitted by
configure when the project uses LT_INIT/AC_PROG_LIBTOOL. Handles the common automake toolchain:
–mode=compile CC … -c src -o obj.lo   -> .libs/obj.o (PIC) + obj.o + obj.lo descriptor
–mode=link    CC … -o lib.la objs     -> .libs/lib.a (static) + .libs/lib.so (shared) + lib.la
–mode=link    CC … -o prog objs *.la  -> resolves .lo/.la and links the program
–mode=install / –mode=clean            -> best-effort copy / rm

# macro_overrides in autoconf_rs_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autoconf-rs-core/0.1.52/autoconf_rs_core/fn.macro_overrides.html

`pub fn macro_overrides() -> &'static `[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)## Expand description

m4 macro definitions injected AFTER aclocal.m4 (so they override the project’s third-party
definitions) and BEFORE configure.ac. autoconf-rs cannot yet correctly expand some standard
third-party macros (notably pkg.m4’s PKG_CHECK_MODULES, whose internals leak
`pkg_default`/`glib_minimum` -> shell syntax errors). We replace them with clean, self-contained
shell that does the real work: run pkg-config at configure time, set PFX_CFLAGS/PFX_LIBS, and
record `@PFX_CFLAGS@`/`@PFX_LIBS@` substitutions into conf_subst.sed (consumed when config files
are created, mirroring confdefs.h -> config.h).

# facett-map3d 0.1.10 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/facett-map3d/0.1.10

**facett-map3d** — a **3D map viewer**: the 2D OSM vector basemap
([`facett_map::Way`]) **extruded into 3D**. Building / area footprints become
**prisms** (a closed ring lifted to a height), line ways become flat **ribbons**
laid on the ground, and the whole map sits on a **terrain plane**. A camera
**orbits** (yaw about Y + a fixed tilt) like [`facett_graph3d::RabbitLogo3D`],
so the city reads as a solid, lit, slowly-turning model.

Two render paths share one [`Facet::ui`] — the same contract as facett-map and
facett-graph3d:

- **CPU painter**(default, always available, headless-testable) — every extruded triangle is projected (orbit yaw + tilt),- **back-face culled**,- **depth sorted**(painter's algorithm), and shaded by- `normal·light`. egui tessellates them, so a host with no wgpu RenderState still gets a real lit 3D map. Never panics.
- **wgpu fast path**(feature- `wgpu`) — reuses facett-graph3d's depth-tested [- `facett_graph3d::logo3d::gpu`] pipeline for the- **znippy rabbit logo overlay**(the spinning mascot in the corner). The basemap prisms always draw on the CPU painter (the headless self-test path), so the GPU is never required.

## The synthetic 3D fixture is the **znippy rabbit** (not squares)

When the host has no real OSM data, [`Map3D::synthetic`] builds the basemap by
**extruding the znippy rabbit silhouette** ([`facett_core::rabbit`]) — each
rabbit loop (body / head / ears) becomes a prism — and pins a 3D
[`facett_graph3d::RabbitLogo3D`] as the logo overlay. So the fixture is a 3D
rabbit-shaped skyline, never a placeholder cube.

# bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1/

## Expand description

This crate gives small utilities for casting between plain data types.

[§](https://docs.rs#basics)Basics

Data comes in five basic forms in Rust, so we have five basic casting functions:

- `T`uses- `cast`
- `&T`uses- `cast_ref`
- `&mut T`uses- `cast_mut`
- `&[T]`uses- `cast_slice`
- `&mut [T]`uses- `cast_slice_mut`

Depending on the function, the [ NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) and/or

[traits are used to maintain memory safety.](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`**Historical Note:** When the crate first started the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait was used
instead, and so you may hear people refer to that, but it has the strongest
requirements and people eventually wanted the more fine-grained system, so
here we are. All types that impl

`Pod` have a blanket impl to also support
`NoUninit` and `AnyBitPattern`. The traits unfortunately do not have a
perfectly clean hierarchy for semver reasons.[§](https://docs.rs#failures)Failures

Some casts will never fail, and other casts might fail.

- `cast::<u32, f32>`always works (and- `f32::from_bits`
- `cast_ref::<[u8; 4], u32>`might fail if the specific array reference given at runtime doesn’t have alignment 4.

In addition to the “normal” forms of each function, which will panic on
invalid input, there’s also `try_` versions which will return a `Result`.

If you would like to statically ensure that a cast will work at runtime you
can use the `must_cast` crate feature and the `must_` casting functions. A
“must cast” that can’t be statically known to be valid will cause a
compilation error (and sometimes a very hard to read compilation error).

[§](https://docs.rs#using-your-own-types)Using Your Own Types

All the functions listed above are guarded by the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait, which is a
sub-trait of the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`If you enable the crate’s `derive` feature then these traits can be derived
on your own types. The derive macros will perform the necessary checks on
your type declaration, and trigger an error if your type does not qualify.

The derive macros might not cover all edge cases, and sometimes they will
error when actually everything is fine. As a last resort you can impl these
traits manually. However, these traits are `unsafe`, and you should
carefully read the requirements before using a manual implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The crate supports Rust 1.34 when no features are enabled, and so there’s cargo features for thing that you might consider “obvious”.

The cargo features **do not** promise any particular MSRV, and they may
increase their MSRV in new versions.

- `derive`: Provide derive macros for the various traits.
- `extern_crate_alloc`: Provide utilities for- `alloc`related types such as Box and Vec.
- `zeroable_maybe_uninit`and- `zeroable_atomics`: Provide more- `Zeroable`
- `pod_saturating`: Provide more- `Pod`- `Zeroable`
- `wasm_simd`and- `aarch64_simd`: Support more SIMD types.
- `min_const_generics`: Provides appropriate impls for arrays of all lengths instead of just for a select list of array lengths.
- `must_cast`: Provides the- `must_`functions, which will compile error if the requested cast can’t be statically verified.
- `const_zeroed`: Provides a const version of the- `zeroed`function.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

- `pack1`- `bytemuck`-compatible packed little-endian, big-endian and native-endian integer and floating point number types.

# egui_wgpu - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/egui-wgpu/^0.34/

## Expand description

This crates provides bindings between [ egui](https://github.com/emilk/egui) and

[wgpu](https://crates.io/crates/wgpu).

If you’re targeting WebGL you also need to turn on the
`webgl` feature of the `wgpu` crate:

```
# Enable both WebGL and WebGPU backends on web.
wgpu = { version = "*", features = ["webgpu", "webgl"] }
```
You can control whether WebGL or WebGPU will be picked at runtime by configuring
[ WgpuConfiguration::wgpu_setup](https://docs.rs/struct.WgpuConfiguration.html#structfield.wgpu_setup).
The default is to prefer WebGPU and fall back on WebGL.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

- `capture`- `capture`module for capturing screenshots.
- `winit`- `winit`- `wayland`or- `x11`
- `wayland`
- `x11`
- `fragile-send-sync-non-atomic-wasm`- *(enabled by default)*— Make the renderer- `Sync`on wasm, exploiting that by default wasm isn’t multithreaded. It may make code easier, especially when targeting both native and web. On native most wgpu objects are send and sync, on the web they are not (by nature of the WebGPU specification). This is not supported in- [multithreaded WASM](https://gpuweb.github.io/gpuweb/explainer/#multithreading-transfer). Thus that usage is guarded against with compiler errors in wgpu.
- `macos-window-resize-jitter-fix`- *(enabled by default)*— Enables- `present_with_transaction`surface flag temporary during window resize on MacOS.

# facett_graph3d - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-graph3d/^0.1/

## Expand description

**facett-graph3d** — a **3D graph viewer**. The idea behind nornir’s
`callgraph.rs` (3D layouts, Y-axis spin, depth cues), rebuilt **generic**:
the consumer supplies `(label, color)` nodes + edges, picks a [ Layout3D](https://docs.rs/enum.Layout3D.html),
and gets a rotating, depth-shaded node cloud. A themed

[.](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html)

`Facet`CPU projection today (orthographic + a Y-rotation, depth → size/brightness); this is exactly the kind of thing the wgpu kernel will accelerate later.

The consumer supplies the graph; the warehouse scanning / theming / projection stay in the host.

# wgpu - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wgpu/^29/

## Expand description

`wgpu` is a cross-platform, safe, pure-Rust graphics API. It runs natively on
Vulkan, Metal, D3D12, and OpenGL; and on top of WebGL2 and WebGPU on wasm.

The API is based on the [WebGPU standard](https://gpuweb.github.io/gpuweb/), but is a fully native Rust library.
It serves as the core of the WebGPU integration in Firefox, Servo, and Deno.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting Started

The main entry point to the API is the [ Instance](https://docs.rs/struct.Instance.html) type, from which you can create

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Adapter.html)

`Adapter`[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Device.html)

`Device`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Surface.html)

`Surface`If you are new to `wgpu` and graphics programming, we recommend starting with [Learn Wgpu](https://sotrh.github.io/learn-wgpu/).

Additionally, [WebGPU Fundamentals](https://webgpufundamentals.org/) is a tutorial for WebGPU which is very similar to our API, minus differences between Rust and Javascript.

We have a [wiki](https://github.com/gfx-rs/wgpu/wiki) which has information on useful architecture patterns, debugging tips, and more getting started information.

There are examples for this version [available on GitHub](https://github.com/gfx-rs/wgpu/tree/v29/examples#readme).

The API is refcounted, so all handles are cloneable, and if you create a resource which references another, it will automatically keep dependent resources alive.

`wgpu` uses the coordinate systems of D3D and Metal. Depth ranges from [0, 1].

| Render | Texture |
|---|---|

`wgpu`’s MSRV is **1.87**.

[§](https://docs.rs#extension-specifications)Extension Specifications

While the core of `wgpu` is based on the WebGPU standard, we also support extensions that allow for features that the standard does not have yet.
For high-level documentation on how to use these extensions, see documentation on [ Features](https://docs.rs/struct.Features.html) or the relevant specification:

🧪EXPERIMENTAL🧪 APIs are subject to change and may allow undefined behavior if used incorrectly.

- 🧪EXPERIMENTAL🧪 [Ray Tracing](https://github.com/gfx-rs/wgpu/blob/v29/docs/api-specs/ray_tracing.md).
- 🧪EXPERIMENTAL🧪 [Mesh Shading](https://github.com/gfx-rs/wgpu/blob/v29/docs/api-specs/mesh_shading.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#shader-support)Shader Support

`wgpu` can consume shaders in [WGSL](https://gpuweb.github.io/gpuweb/wgsl/), SPIR-V, and GLSL.
Both [HLSL](https://github.com/Microsoft/DirectXShaderCompiler) and [GLSL](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glslang)
have compilers to target SPIR-V. All of these shader languages can be used with any backend as we handle all of the conversions. Additionally, support for these shader inputs is not going away.

While WebGPU does not support any shading language other than WGSL, we will automatically convert your non-WGSL shaders if you’re running on WebGPU.

WGSL is always supported by default, but GLSL and SPIR-V need features enabled to compile in support.

To enable WGSL shaders, enable the `wgsl` feature of `wgpu` (enabled by default).
To enable SPIR-V shaders, enable the `spirv` feature of `wgpu`.
To enable GLSL shaders, enable the `glsl` feature of `wgpu`.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

[§](https://docs.rs#backends)Backends

- `dx12`- *(enabled by default)*— Enables the DX12 backend on Windows.
- `metal`- *(enabled by default)*— Enables the Metal backend on macOS & iOS.
- `vulkan`- *(enabled by default)*— Enables the Vulkan backend on Windows, Linux, and Android.
- `gles`- *(enabled by default)*— Enables the OpenGL/GLES backend on Windows, Linux, Android, and Emscripten.
- `webgpu`- *(enabled by default)*— Enables the WebGPU backend on WebAssembly.

[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-backends)Conditional Backends

-
`angle`[ANGLE](https://github.com/google/angle).
-
`vulkan-portability`[MoltenVK](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/MoltenVK).
-
`webgl`
-
`noop`This backend allows creating resources such as buffers and textures, but performs no computation. Because it lacks basic functionality, it is only actually used if explicitly enabled through `NoopBackendOptions`.

**Note:** In the documentation, if you see that an item depends on a backend,
it means that the item is only available when that backend is enabled *and* the backend
is supported on the current platform.

[§](https://docs.rs#shading-language-support)Shading language support

These features enable support for that input language on all platforms. We will translate the input language to whatever the backend requires.

- `spirv`
- `glsl`
- `wgsl`- *(enabled by default)*— Enable accepting WGSL shaders as input.
- `naga-ir`

[§](https://docs.rs#assertions-and-serialization)Assertions and Serialization

- `strict_asserts`
- `serde`- `serde`on common wgpu types.

[§](https://docs.rs#external-libraries)External libraries

The following features facilitate integration with third-party supporting libraries.

-
`static-dxc`Normally, to use the modern DXC shader compiler with wgpu, the final application must be shipped alongside `dxcompiler.dll`(min v1.8.2502) (which can be downloaded from[Microsoft’s GitHub](https://github.com/Microsoft/DirectXShaderCompiler)). This feature statically links a version of DXC so that no external binaries are required to compile DX12 shaders.

[§](https://docs.rs#other)Other

-
`counters`
-
`fragile-send-sync-non-atomic-wasm``Send`and`Sync`on Wasm, but only if atomics are not enabled.WebGL/WebGPU objects can not be shared between threads. However, it can be useful to artificially mark them as `Send`and`Sync`anyways to make it easier to write cross-platform code. This is technically*very*unsafe in a multithreaded environment, but on a wasm binary compiled without atomics is a definitionally single-threaded environment.
-
`web`*(enabled by default)*— Use web-specific libraries on WASMThose libraries (wasm-bindgen, web-sys, js-sys) can only be used when there is a JavaScript context around the WASM VM, e.g., when the WASM binary is used in a browser.
-
`std`*(enabled by default)*— Enables use of the standard library within`wgpu`and its dependencies.This can allow for better error reporting and for improved multithreading support.
-
`parking_lot`*(enabled by default)*— Uses`parking_lot`as the implementation for locking primitives.This is a recommended feature for most users and should only be disabled when required, e.g., for `no_std`support. If disabled, either`std::sync::Mutex`or`core::cell::RefCell`will be used, based on whether`std`is enabled or not.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-aliases)Feature Aliases

These features aren’t actually features on the crate itself, but a convenient shorthand for complicated cases.

- `wgpu_core`
- `naga`- `glsl`or- `spirv`input is enabled, or when- `wgpu_core`is enabled.

# facett_map3d - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/facett-map3d/0.1.10/target-redirect/facett_map3d/

## Expand description

**facett-map3d** — a **3D map viewer**: the 2D OSM vector basemap
([ facett_map::Way](https://docs.rs/facett-map/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_map/struct.Way.html))

**extruded into 3D**. Building / area footprints become

**prisms**(a closed ring lifted to a height), line ways become flat

**ribbons**laid on the ground, and the whole map sits on a

**terrain plane**. A camera

**orbits**(yaw about Y + a fixed tilt) like

[, so the city reads as a solid, lit, slowly-turning model.](https://docs.rs/struct.RabbitLogo3D.html)

`facett_graph3d::RabbitLogo3D`Two render paths share one [ Facet::ui](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html#tymethod.ui) — the same contract as facett-map and
facett-graph3d:

- **CPU painter**(default, always available, headless-testable) — every extruded triangle is projected (orbit yaw + tilt),- **back-face culled**,- **depth sorted**(painter’s algorithm), and shaded by- `normal·light`. egui tessellates them, so a host with no wgpu RenderState still gets a real lit 3D map. Never panics.
- **wgpu fast path**(feature- `wgpu`) — reuses facett-graph3d’s depth-tested [- `facett_graph3d::logo3d::gpu`] pipeline for the- **znippy rabbit logo overlay**(the spinning mascot in the corner). The basemap prisms always draw on the CPU painter (the headless self-test path), so the GPU is never required.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-synthetic-3d-fixture-is-the-znippy-rabbit-not-squares)The synthetic 3D fixture is the **znippy rabbit** (not squares)

When the host has no real OSM data, [ Map3D::synthetic](https://docs.rs/struct.Map3D.html#method.synthetic) builds the basemap by

**extruding the znippy rabbit silhouette**(

[) — each rabbit loop (body / head / ears) becomes a prism — and pins a 3D](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/rabbit/index.html)

`facett_core::rabbit`[as the logo overlay. So the fixture is a 3D rabbit-shaped skyline, never a placeholder cube.](https://docs.rs/struct.RabbitLogo3D.html)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [camera](https://docs.rs/camera/index.html)
- **OrbitCamera**— a state-of-the-art, fully navigable 3D camera for the OSM viewer. The camera orbits a- **target**point on spherical coordinates (azimuth + elevation + distance), like three.js- `OrbitControls`/- `camera-controls`and Blender’s turntable: drag to orbit, wheel to- **dolly toward the cursor**, middle/shift-drag to- **pan**, and snap to canonical- **view-angle presets**(top-down / iso / oblique / front).
- [extrude](https://docs.rs/extrude/index.html)
- **Extrusion**— turn 2D OSM ways (- `facett_map::Way`- `[-1, 1]`design box (the same box- `facett_core::rabbit`
- [lod](https://docs.rs/lod/index.html)
- Altitude / LOD lever + the `METRES_PER_DESIGN_UNIT`calibration (the headline`< 300 m → reflective water`trigger). Pure CPU, inject-assert-testable.**Altitude / LOD lever + the metre calibration**— the single CPU lever that turns the camera’s design-unit dolly distance into a real-world**altitude in metres**, then resolves a`LodTier``< 300 m → reflective water`rule is just one threshold of this lever.
- [sky](https://docs.rs/sky/index.html)
- Sun + sky lighting model (Phase 1) shared by the GPU PBR shader + CPU painter.
**Sun + sky lighting model**(Phase 1) — the single source of truth for the directional sun, its colour/intensity, and the sky/ambient tint, shared by the GPU PBR shader (`map3d.wgsl`) and the CPU painter so both render paths agree.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [clip_](https://docs.rs/fn.clip_poly_to_rect.html)- poly_ - to_ - rect
- **Sutherland–Hodgman**clip of a triangle to an axis-aligned- `rect`— the CPU painter’s- **scissor**.- **Moved to**(CONS-CORE Phase A, step 3) and re-exported here so map3d’s public API + its regression fence (- `facett_core::render::cpu::scissor`- `clip_pipeline`/- `frustum_scissor`/- `no_spokes`/- `near_plane_probe`/- `gpu_scissor`) are unchanged. The move is behavior-preserving.- **Sutherland–Hodgman**clip of a triangle (- `tri`) to an axis-aligned- `rect`, returning the clipped convex polygon’s vertices (3..=7 of them) or an empty Vec when the triangle lies wholly outside the rect. This is the CPU painter’s- **scissor**: it geometrically confines every face to the widget rect so nothing a 3D/2D pass paints can land outside the component’s own rectangle — independent of whether the host renderer applies the egui clip_rect as a GPU scissor.
- [clip_](https://docs.rs/fn.clip_tri_frustum.html)- tri_ - frustum
- **Full view-space FRUSTUM clip**(the real fix for the smear) — Sutherland–Hodgman of a triangle against all FIVE relevant frustum planes BEFORE the perspective divide: the near plane- `z >= near`AND the four side planes- `|cx| <= cz·sx`,- `|cy| <= cz·sy`(with- `sx`,- `sy`the projection’s per-axis NDC slopes — for- `project_view`’s focal =- `half_h`,- `sy = 1`,- `sx = half_w/half_h`).
- [clip_](https://docs.rs/fn.clip_tri_near.html)- tri_ - near
- **View-space near-plane clip**(step 1 of the part-step decomposition) — Sutherland–Hodgman clip of a single view-space triangle against the half-space- `z >= near`, returning the clipped convex polygon’s view-space vertices (0 when the whole triangle sits on/behind the eye, 3 when untouched, 4 when one vertex was behind and split). This runs- **before**the perspective divide so no surviving vertex ever divides by a near-zero / negative depth — the geometric replacement for the old “near-singularity spoke reject” + “screen-extent guard” heuristics that let off-axis near faces smear thousands of px off the rect.
- [ink_](https://docs.rs/fn.ink_outside_rect.html)- outside_ - rect
- **Sutherland–Hodgman**clip of a triangle to an axis-aligned- `rect`— the CPU painter’s- **scissor**.- **Moved to**(CONS-CORE Phase A, step 3) and re-exported here so map3d’s public API + its regression fence (- `facett_core::render::cpu::scissor`- `clip_pipeline`/- `frustum_scissor`/- `no_spokes`/- `near_plane_probe`/- `gpu_scissor`) are unchanged. The move is behavior-preserving. The scissor- **oracle**(- `scissor.ink_outside_rect`): count the vertices of the- *scissored*polygons that still land outside- `rect`(beyond- `eps`). A correct scissor leaves- **0**— this is the bug oracle the spec’s clip stage emits (- `ink_outside_rect == 0`). Pure, so both the emit path and tests call it.
- [scissor_](https://docs.rs/fn.scissor_report.html)- report
- **Scissor oracle**(step 7) — measure how far the faces overshoot the widget rect- *before*the rect-scissor confines them, and confirm the clipped output never lands outside. Returns- `(raw_overshoot_px, clipped_escapes)`:

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [camera](https://docs.rs/camera/index.html)
- **OrbitCamera**— a state-of-the-art, fully navigable 3D camera for the OSM viewer. The camera orbits a- **target**point on spherical coordinates (azimuth + elevation + distance), like three.js- `OrbitControls`/- `camera-controls`and Blender’s turntable: drag to orbit, wheel to- **dolly toward the cursor**, middle/shift-drag to- **pan**, and snap to canonical- **view-angle presets**(top-down / iso / oblique / front).
- [extrude](https://docs.rs/extrude/index.html)
- **Extrusion**— turn 2D OSM ways (- `facett_map::Way`- `[-1, 1]`design box (the same box- `facett_core::rabbit`
- [lod](https://docs.rs/lod/index.html)
- Altitude / LOD lever + the `METRES_PER_DESIGN_UNIT`calibration (the headline`< 300 m → reflective water`trigger). Pure CPU, inject-assert-testable.**Altitude / LOD lever + the metre calibration**— the single CPU lever that turns the camera’s design-unit dolly distance into a real-world**altitude in metres**, then resolves a`LodTier``< 300 m → reflective water`rule is just one threshold of this lever.
- [sky](https://docs.rs/sky/index.html)
- Sun + sky lighting model (Phase 1) shared by the GPU PBR shader + CPU painter.
**Sun + sky lighting model**(Phase 1) — the single source of truth for the directional sun, its colour/intensity, and the sky/ambient tint, shared by the GPU PBR shader (`map3d.wgsl`) and the CPU painter so both render paths agree.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [clip_](https://docs.rs/fn.clip_poly_to_rect.html)- poly_ - to_ - rect
- **Sutherland–Hodgman**clip of a triangle to an axis-aligned- `rect`— the CPU painter’s- **scissor**.- **Moved to**(CONS-CORE Phase A, step 3) and re-exported here so map3d’s public API + its regression fence (- `facett_core::render::cpu::scissor`- `clip_pipeline`/- `frustum_scissor`/- `no_spokes`/- `near_plane_probe`/- `gpu_scissor`) are unchanged. The move is behavior-preserving.- **Sutherland–Hodgman**clip of a triangle (- `tri`) to an axis-aligned- `rect`, returning the clipped convex polygon’s vertices (3..=7 of them) or an empty Vec when the triangle lies wholly outside the rect. This is the CPU painter’s- **scissor**: it geometrically confines every face to the widget rect so nothing a 3D/2D pass paints can land outside the component’s own rectangle — independent of whether the host renderer applies the egui clip_rect as a GPU scissor.
- [clip_](https://docs.rs/fn.clip_tri_frustum.html)- tri_ - frustum
- **Full view-space FRUSTUM clip**(the real fix for the smear) — Sutherland–Hodgman of a triangle against all FIVE relevant frustum planes BEFORE the perspective divide: the near plane- `z >= near`AND the four side planes- `|cx| <= cz·sx`,- `|cy| <= cz·sy`(with- `sx`,- `sy`the projection’s per-axis NDC slopes — for- `project_view`’s focal =- `half_h`,- `sy = 1`,- `sx = half_w/half_h`).
- [clip_](https://docs.rs/fn.clip_tri_near.html)- tri_ - near
- **View-space near-plane clip**(step 1 of the part-step decomposition) — Sutherland–Hodgman clip of a single view-space triangle against the half-space- `z >= near`, returning the clipped convex polygon’s view-space vertices (0 when the whole triangle sits on/behind the eye, 3 when untouched, 4 when one vertex was behind and split). This runs- **before**the perspective divide so no surviving vertex ever divides by a near-zero / negative depth — the geometric replacement for the old “near-singularity spoke reject” + “screen-extent guard” heuristics that let off-axis near faces smear thousands of px off the rect.
- [ink_](https://docs.rs/fn.ink_outside_rect.html)- outside_ - rect
- **Sutherland–Hodgman**clip of a triangle to an axis-aligned- `rect`— the CPU painter’s- **scissor**.- **Moved to**(CONS-CORE Phase A, step 3) and re-exported here so map3d’s public API + its regression fence (- `facett_core::render::cpu::scissor`- `clip_pipeline`/- `frustum_scissor`/- `no_spokes`/- `near_plane_probe`/- `gpu_scissor`) are unchanged. The move is behavior-preserving. The scissor- **oracle**(- `scissor.ink_outside_rect`): count the vertices of the- *scissored*polygons that still land outside- `rect`(beyond- `eps`). A correct scissor leaves- **0**— this is the bug oracle the spec’s clip stage emits (- `ink_outside_rect == 0`). Pure, so both the emit path and tests call it.
- [scissor_](https://docs.rs/fn.scissor_report.html)- report
- **Scissor oracle**(step 7) — measure how far the faces overshoot the widget rect- *before*the rect-scissor confines them, and confirm the clipped output never lands outside. Returns- `(raw_overshoot_px, clipped_escapes)`:

# facett_map3d/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! **facett-map3d** — a **3D map viewer**: the 2D OSM vector basemap
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! ([`facett_map::Way`]) **extruded into 3D**. Building / area footprints become
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! **prisms** (a closed ring lifted to a height), line ways become flat **ribbons**
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! laid on the ground, and the whole map sits on a **terrain plane**. A camera
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! **orbits** (yaw about Y + a fixed tilt) like [`facett_graph3d::RabbitLogo3D`],
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! so the city reads as a solid, lit, slowly-turning model.
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! Two render paths share one [`Facet::ui`] — the same contract as facett-map and
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! facett-graph3d:
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! - **CPU painter** (default, always available, headless-testable) — every
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!   extruded triangle is projected (orbit yaw + tilt), **back-face culled**,
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!   **depth sorted** (painter's algorithm), and shaded by `normal·light`. egui
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!   tessellates them, so a host with no wgpu RenderState still gets a real lit
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!   3D map. Never panics.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! - **wgpu fast path** (feature `wgpu`) — reuses facett-graph3d's depth-tested
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!   [`facett_graph3d::logo3d::gpu`] pipeline for the **znippy rabbit logo overlay**
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!   (the spinning mascot in the corner). The basemap prisms always draw on the
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!   CPU painter (the headless self-test path), so the GPU is never required.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! ## The synthetic 3D fixture is the **znippy rabbit** (not squares)
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! When the host has no real OSM data, [`Map3D::synthetic`] builds the basemap by
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! **extruding the znippy rabbit silhouette** ([`facett_core::rabbit`]) — each
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! rabbit loop (body / head / ears) becomes a prism — and pins a 3D
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! [`facett_graph3d::RabbitLogo3D`] as the logo overlay. So the fixture is a 3D
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! rabbit-shaped skyline, never a placeholder cube.
[27](https://docs.rs#27)

[140](https://docs.rs#140)impl Map3D {

[142](https://docs.rs#142)    /// area/building rings are extruded to prisms; line ways become ground ribbons;
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    /// a terrain plane is fitted under the data. `height` is the design-space lift
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    /// applied to area rings (≈0.18 looks like a chunky city).

[149](https://docs.rs#149)        cam.settle();
[150](https://docs.rs#150)        Self {
[151](https://docs.rs#151)            title: title.into(),
[152](https://docs.rs#152)            mesh,
[153](https://docs.rs#153)            tile_count,
[154](https://docs.rs#154)            logo: None,
[155](https://docs.rs#155)            yaw: 0.6,
[156](https://docs.rs#156)            tilt: 0.55,
[157](https://docs.rs#157)            spin: true,
[158](https://docs.rs#158)            spin_rate: 0.3,
[159](https://docs.rs#159)            clock_s: None,
[160](https://docs.rs#160)            cam,
[161](https://docs.rs#161)            fps: 0.0,
[162](https://docs.rs#162)            last_visible_tris: 0,
[163](https://docs.rs#163)            #[cfg(feature = "wgpu")]
[164](https://docs.rs#164)            use_gpu: false,
[165](https://docs.rs#165)            #[cfg(feature = "wgpu")]
[166](https://docs.rs#166)            gpu_geom: None,
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            last_used_gpu: false,
[168](https://docs.rs#168)            metres_per_du,
[169](https://docs.rs#169)            last_tier_ground: false,
[170](https://docs.rs#170)            sun: SunSky::noon(),
[171](https://docs.rs#171)            #[cfg(feature = "wgpu")]
[172](https://docs.rs#172)            shadow_strength: 0.85,
[173](https://docs.rs#173)            water,
[174](https://docs.rs#174)            water_override: None,
[175](https://docs.rs#175)            planar_reflection: true,
[176](https://docs.rs#176)            #[cfg(feature = "wgpu")]

[332](https://docs.rs#332)
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    /// **Real-data constructor** — build a 3D city from pre-loaded OSM
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    /// [`Way`]s (the host reads `ways.parquet` via `facett-osm`). A convenience
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    /// alias for [`Self::from_ways`] with the standard city extrusion height,
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    /// named for intent at the demo's OSM 3D tab call site. Empty ways → just the
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// terrain plane (graceful).
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    pub fn from_geometry(title: impl Into<String>, ways: &[Way]) -> Self {
[339](https://docs.rs#339)        // **Subset to one town first**, THEN extrude. A country-/region-scale load
[340](https://docs.rs#340)        // (e.g. all of liechtenstein, ~30 km) has sub-pixel footprints and, once
[341](https://docs.rs#341)        // dollied into, a giant terrain plane whose far edges starburst. Extruding
[342](https://docs.rs#342)        // only the densest ~3 km town makes the mesh city-scale: building heights
[343](https://docs.rs#343)        // scale to the town span (a readable skyline), the terrain is town-sized
[344](https://docs.rs#344)        // (no far spokes), and a normal camera frames it. A load that is already a
[345](https://docs.rs#345)        // single town (or the synthetic fixture) is returned unchanged.
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        let town = extrude::densest_cluster_subset(ways);
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        let mut m = Self::from_ways(title, &town, 0.22);
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        // Still aim at the densest sub-cluster + dolly so the town fills the view.
[349](https://docs.rs#349)        m.frame_densest_cluster();
[350](https://docs.rs#350)        m
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    }
[352](https://docs.rs#352)
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    /// Find the **densest cluster of risen (building) geometry** in the extruded
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    /// mesh and point the camera at it, dollied in so the cluster fills the view.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    /// Buildings are the `y > 0` (lifted) vertices; ground cover / terrain lie flat
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    /// at `y = 0`. We bin the risen vertices into a coarse grid, pick the heaviest
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    /// cell, then set the camera target to that cell's centroid and the distance to
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    /// the cluster's extent — so a country-scale dataset still shows a real town.
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    pub fn frame_densest_cluster(&mut self) {
[360](https://docs.rs#360)        // Collect risen (building) vertices in the ground (x,z) plane.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)        let risen: Vec<[f32; 3]> = self.mesh.positions.iter().copied().filter(|p| p[1] > 1e-3).collect();
[362](https://docs.rs#362)        if risen.len() < 3 {
[363](https://docs.rs#363)            return; // nothing risen (all flat) → keep the default whole-box framing
[364](https://docs.rs#364)        }
[365](https://docs.rs#365)        // Bin into a GRID×GRID grid over the design box [-1,1]² and find the
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        // heaviest cell (the densest town).
[367](https://docs.rs#367)        const GRID: usize = 24;
[368](https://docs.rs#368)        let cell = |v: f32| (((v + 1.0) * 0.5 * GRID as f32) as usize).min(GRID - 1);
[369](https://docs.rs#369)        let mut bins = vec![0u32; GRID * GRID];
[370](https://docs.rs#370)        for p in &risen {
[371](https://docs.rs#371)            bins[cell(p[2]) * GRID + cell(p[0])] += 1;
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        }
[373](https://docs.rs#373)        let (best, _) = bins.iter().enumerate().max_by_key(|(_, c)| **c).unwrap();
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        let (bz, bx) = (best / GRID, best % GRID);
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        // Cluster = the best cell + its 8 neighbours. Centroid + extent of the
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        // risen verts that fall inside that 3×3 neighbourhood.
[377](https://docs.rs#377)        let in_cluster = |p: &[f32; 3]| {
[378](https://docs.rs#378)            let (cx, cz) = (cell(p[0]) as isize, cell(p[2]) as isize);
[379](https://docs.rs#379)            (cx - bx as isize).abs() <= 1 && (cz - bz as isize).abs() <= 1
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        };
[381](https://docs.rs#381)        let mut cnt = 0.0f32;
[382](https://docs.rs#382)        let (mut sx, mut sz) = (0.0f32, 0.0f32);
[383](https://docs.rs#383)        let (mut x0, mut z0, mut x1, mut z1) = (f32::MAX, f32::MAX, f32::MIN, f32::MIN);
[384](https://docs.rs#384)        let mut ymax = 0.0f32;
[385](https://docs.rs#385)        for p in risen.iter().filter(|p| in_cluster(p)) {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)            sx += p[0];
[387](https://docs.rs#387)            sz += p[2];
[388](https://docs.rs#388)            cnt += 1.0;
[389](https://docs.rs#389)            x0 = x0.min(p[0]);
[390](https://docs.rs#390)            z0 = z0.min(p[2]);
[391](https://docs.rs#391)            x1 = x1.max(p[0]);
[392](https://docs.rs#392)            z1 = z1.max(p[2]);
[393](https://docs.rs#393)            ymax = ymax.max(p[1]);
[394](https://docs.rs#394)        }
[395](https://docs.rs#395)        if cnt < 1.0 {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)            return;
[397](https://docs.rs#397)        }
[398](https://docs.rs#398)        let (tx, tz) = (sx / cnt, sz / cnt);
[399](https://docs.rs#399)        let extent = (x1 - x0).max(z1 - z0).max(0.05);
[400](https://docs.rs#400)        // Distance so the cluster fills roughly the vertical fov; clamp to the
[401](https://docs.rs#401)        // camera's dolly range so it never clips through or flies away.
[402](https://docs.rs#402)        let dist = (extent / (self.cam.fov_y * 0.5).tan() * 1.6).clamp(self.cam.min_distance, self.cam.max_distance);
[403](https://docs.rs#403)        self.cam.target = V3::new(tx, ymax * 0.4, tz);
[404](https://docs.rs#404)        self.cam.goal_target = self.cam.target;
[405](https://docs.rs#405)        self.cam.distance = dist;
[406](https://docs.rs#406)        self.cam.goal_distance = dist;
[407](https://docs.rs#407)        // A pleasant oblique 3/4 view of the town.
[408](https://docs.rs#408)        self.cam.apply_preset(ViewPreset::Oblique);
[409](https://docs.rs#409)        self.cam.settle();
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    }
